title: Chapter 9. What Does Not Come Back

blocks.text: Nothing is lost, said the phrase, and yet there were things that didn't come back.
blocks.html: Nothing is lost, said the phrase, and yet there were things that didn't come back.

blocks.text: Vicente didn't come back. His order, if it could ever have been named, was no longer in any machine: he had come to his end in his own time, with his straw hat and his cistern, and the door was still shut, not to tidy up the landscape but out of fidelity. Andrés passed in front of it one evening, after having crossed and come back, and didn't open it. He spoke to him, the way people in Lo Pagán speak to the absent, without asking doctrine for permission.

blocks.text: “You're not in a hangar,” he said. “You're not in a circle. Your energy, if the phrase is true, is still somewhere, turned into something else, into earth, into heat, into a tomato that's no longer on your windowsill. But you, the man of the house, aren't coming back. I've come back from a hollow. That doesn't reach you. Forgive me for having a machine when all you had was a time.”

blocks.text: That week Helena climbed her stairs more slowly and refused, for the last time or one more time, the offer of a transfer that would give her back the knees of twenty years ago. “No improvement,” they told her, or “a little, if you like”. She laughed, briefly, as when Aya had told her about the bridge.

blocks.text: “If you put me together better, I won't be climbing these stairs any more,” she said. “And these stairs are the only thing I have that doesn't belong to the company. Tell them, the people on the shore, that some don't come back because they don't want to, not because they can't.”

blocks.text: Aya passed it on, on her behalf, in the kitchen. Lía heard it and nodded, the stone from the mountains now accustomed to its furrow.
blocks.html: Aya passed it on, on her behalf, in the kitchen. Lía heard it and nodded, the stone from the mountains now accustomed to its furrow.

blocks.text: “The machine doesn't give back the whiles,” she said. “It gives back, if it gets it right, an order. Vicente's while, the while of Helena's stairs, my winter's, Mother's on the doorstep as the boat grows small: those aren't named in a curve. That's why, Father, ‘nothing is lost’ is true of matter and a lie about lives, or not a lie: a narrower truth than it seems. What can be measured is conserved. What is loved is interrupted.”

blocks.text: Andrés, who had been a hollow and then a place again, didn't argue. He sat by the wrong clock and looked at its two minutes' slowness, which no Madrid machine had set right, this time.

blocks.text: “Then what do we do with the phrase?” he asked. “Do we take it off the door?”
blocks.html: “Then what do we do with the phrase?” he asked. “Do we take it off the door?”

blocks.text: “We leave it, with a second line,” said Lía, as in the priceless garden. “Nothing is lost, in weight, in heat, in the order that can be named. And underneath: some whiles don't travel. Ask for the journey, if you ask for it, knowing that. Don't impose it. Don't sell it as a smoother eternity.”

blocks.text: Aya wrote the two lines in her own hand on a sheet of paper and put them near the cup that had crossed, not as a company sign but as a kitchen notice. The technician, when he read them, asked to take a copy to the warehouse, and they gave him one, and he didn't “improve” it.

blocks.text: The one who searches answered in a letter from a new world, one that had no children yet, or was beginning to have them:
blocks.html: The one who searches answered in a letter from a new world, one that had no children yet, or was beginning to have them:

blocks.text: *I've heard the two lines. I'll have them said in the hangar. I'm still searching, and sometimes I cross, and sometimes I don't. I won't put together those who have come to an end. I'm not an owner of the absent. If one day I stop searching, I'll come to your door, not to a laboratory, to see whether the coffee has gone too cold.*

blocks.text: Andrés kept that letter the way you keep a rope. At night the three of them (and Iago, for a while) had their tea without a machine, without a visiting people, with a tomato from the plot and a home silence. That silence didn't travel. That was why it was theirs.

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If matter isn't lost and a man is, which of the two truths should rule in a kitchen? And if a shut door is what doesn't come back, isn't it also, precisely, what allows whatever does come back to have somewhere to come back to?*
blocks.html: If matter isn't lost and a man is, which of the two truths should rule in a kitchen? And if a shut door is what doesn't come back, isn't it also, precisely, what allows whatever does come back to have somewhere to come back to?

blocks.text: MAY, without judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, without judgment:

blocks.text: *Vicente has not been put together again. Helena has refused a transfer that would improve her knees. Two lines have been written: nothing is lost, in what can be measured; some whiles do not travel. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: Before sleeping, Andrés stayed on the doorstep and crossed nowhere. The Mar Menor barely lapped, ancient, the same murmur as in 2026, in 2060, in the letters, in the peoples, in the hollow. He thought that water too comes apart, wave after wave, and comes back, and isn't the same, and is the same, and nobody in Lo Pagán asks the wave to swear to its identity. They ask only that it arrive, and leave, and not stop being this shore. That, which wasn't laboratory physics, was enough for him that night not to fear the doubt so much, nor to have so much faith in the phrase, and still to love the cup that hadn't travelled, beside the one that had, in a single sink, without either of them gaining more than its share.

blocks.text: The next day Lía went to Vicente's door with an ordinary tomato, not a healing one, and left it on the windowsill, knowing it would wrinkle. It wasn't to bring him back. It was so that the absence would have, for one more day, its honest fruit, the kind that isn't put together on the other side. Andrés saw her and said nothing. Nor did Aya, from the window. In Lo Pagán, sometimes, what doesn't come back is honoured like this: with something that also comes to an end, set in the sun, without a machine and without a report.

blocks.text: A boy from the gardens asked, as he went by, whether it could be eaten. Lía said yes, when it ripened, if he asked for it, and if not, let it stay for the windowsill. The boy nodded and didn't take it yet. That small wait was also a while that didn't travel, and for that reason, on this shore, it mattered.
